text: Three terms used interchangeably in conversation, genuinely distinct in practice. Locking is the mechanism. Blocking is the consequence becoming visible. A deadlock is the one failure mode SQL Server can't resolve on its own.

Locking is always happening, mostly invisible, mostly healthy -- shared locks for reads, exclusive for writes, at row, page, or table level. sys.dm_tran_locks shows every lock held, and a WAIT status row is a session blocked right now.

Blocking itself is normal -- the problem is a chain that lasts long enough for users to notice. blocking_session_id tells you who's holding the lock. Chase that chain back to the session with blocking_session_id equal to zero -- the actual root cause.

A deadlock is specifically circular -- two sessions each waiting on a lock the other holds. Neither can proceed, so SQL Server kills a chosen victim to break the cycle. DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW makes a session more likely to be picked.

Shorter transactions, consistent access order, and the right indexes reduce lock contention, blocking, and deadlocks all at once. Next up: the query-performance-specific DMVs, distinct from Chapter 7's general monitoring coverage.
